items.title: Physics I — Units, Motion, Force, Gravitation & Fluids
items.body:
### Units, motion and force

**In one line**
This is the grammar of physics: the units we measure in, how we describe moving bodies, and the three Newton rules that say why they move.

**The story**
Every measurement needs an agreed yardstick. Scientists agreed on **seven base units** — everything else (force, energy, power) is built from them, so these are called *derived* units. Once you can measure length and time you can describe **motion**: how fast (speed), how fast and in which direction (velocity), and how quickly the velocity changes (acceleration). Newton then explained *why* motion changes: a body keeps doing what it is doing unless a force acts (first law), a force changes its motion in proportion to the force and inversely to its mass (second law, F = ma), and every push produces an equal push back (third law).

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
APPSC repeatedly asks SI base-vs-derived units, scalar-vs-vector sorting, and one-line statements of Newton's laws. These are single-fact or multi-statement items that are easy marks if the definitions are crisp.

**Picture it**

| Topic | Key facts |
|---|---|
| Seven base units | metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount), candela (luminous intensity) |
| Derived units | newton (force), joule (energy), watt (power), pascal (pressure), hertz (frequency) |
| Scalars (size only) | distance, speed, mass, energy |
| Vectors (size + direction) | displacement, velocity, acceleration, force |
| Newton's laws | 1 = inertia · 2 = F = ma · 3 = equal and opposite forces on two different bodies |

**Terms explained**
- **Scalar** — a quantity with size only (speed = 60 km/h).
- **Vector** — a quantity with size and direction (velocity = 60 km/h north).
- **Inertia** — the tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of rest or motion.
- **Momentum** — mass multiplied by velocity; it is conserved (stays the same total) in collisions.
- **g** — acceleration due to gravity, about 9.8 metres per second each second near Earth's surface.

**Equations of motion** (straight line, constant acceleration): v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as, where u = starting speed, v = final speed, a = acceleration, t = time, s = distance.

### Gravitation and fluids

**The story (continued)**
Gravity pulls every mass towards every other mass (Newton's universal law, F = G·m₁m₂ divided by r²). Near Earth this gives the value **g**. Because Earth is slightly flattened, you are a little closer to the centre at the poles, so g is a touch larger there (about 9.83) than at the equator (about 9.78). Your **mass** never changes, but your **weight** (W = mg) does, because it depends on g — on the Moon g is only one-sixth, so you weigh one-sixth as much. In liquids and gases, Archimedes saw that a submerged body is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of fluid it shoves aside; if that upward push can balance the body's weight, the body floats.

**Picture it**

| Idea | Rule |
|---|---|
| Value of g | greater at poles (~9.83) than equator (~9.78); one-sixth on the Moon; zero at Earth's centre |
| Weight vs mass | mass constant everywhere; weight W = mg varies with g |
| Pressure in a fluid | P = hρg — rises with depth; atmospheric pressure ≈ 101 kilopascals at sea level, falls with altitude |
| Archimedes' principle | upthrust = weight of fluid displaced; a body floats when its average density is less than the fluid's |
| Work and power | Work = force × distance × cosθ (zero when force is at right angles to movement); Power = work ÷ time (watt); 1 horsepower ≈ 746 watts |

**Don't confuse**
- **Mass vs weight** — mass is the amount of matter (kilograms, constant); weight is the gravitational pull on it (newtons, changes with g).
- **Speed vs velocity** — speed has no direction; velocity does, so a body in a circle at steady speed still has changing velocity.
- **Third law bodies** — action and reaction are equal and opposite but act on *two different* bodies, so they never cancel out.

**Remember it**
Newton in order is "**1-2-3 = Inertia, F = ma, Pairs**"; and "a ship floats because it pushes aside more water-weight than it weighs".

**TL;DR**
- Seven SI base units; newton/joule/watt/pascal are derived.
- Displacement, velocity, acceleration, force are vectors; distance, speed, mass are scalars.
- Newton: inertia → F = ma → equal-opposite pairs on different bodies; momentum = mass × velocity.
- g is bigger at the poles and one-sixth on the Moon; weight changes with g, mass does not.
- Archimedes: upthrust = weight of displaced fluid; float when density < fluid's; 1 HP ≈ 746 W.
keyPoints: Seven SI base units include kelvin (temperature) and mole (amount); newton/joule/watt are derived.
Displacement, velocity and acceleration are vectors; distance and speed are scalars.
Newton's 1st law = inertia; 2nd law F = ma; 3rd law action-reaction act on different bodies.
Momentum = mass × velocity and is conserved in collisions.
g is greater at the poles than the equator and about one-sixth on the Moon; weight = mg, mass is constant.
Work = force × distance × cosθ (zero when force is perpendicular to displacement); 1 horsepower ≈ 746 watts.
Archimedes' principle: upthrust = weight of displaced fluid; a body floats if its density < fluid's; pressure P = hρg.
items.source: NCERT Science Class 9 — Motion; Force and Laws of Motion; Gravitation; Work and Energy

items.title: Physics II — Light, Sound & Heat
items.body:
### Light — mirrors, lenses and colour

**In one line**
Light bounces off surfaces (reflection) and bends when it changes medium (refraction), and these two behaviours explain mirrors, spectacles and the rainbow.

**The story**
When light hits a smooth surface it bounces off at the same angle it arrived — the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. A **concave** mirror curves inward and brings rays together (converging), so it is used in torches, headlights and shaving mirrors; a **convex** mirror curves outward and spreads rays (diverging), giving a small upright image and a wide view, which is why it is the vehicle rear-view mirror. When light passes from air into glass or water it bends — this is refraction. A **convex lens** is fat in the middle and converges light (a magnifying glass; corrects long sight); a **concave lens** is thin in the middle and diverges light (corrects short sight). A glass prism bends the colours of white light by different amounts, splitting it into the familiar sequence red-to-violet — this spreading is called dispersion, and the rainbow is dispersion plus reflection inside raindrops.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
Mirror and lens type (converging vs diverging), the rear-view-mirror example, eye-defect corrections and the word 'dispersion' are classic single-fact and statement MCQs.

**Picture it**

| Device | Behaviour | Everyday use |
|---|---|---|
| Concave mirror | converges | headlights, shaving mirror |
| Convex mirror | diverges | rear-view mirror (wide view) |
| Convex lens | converges | magnifying glass; corrects hypermetropia (long sight) |
| Concave lens | diverges | corrects myopia (short sight) |

### Sound and heat

**The story (continued)**
Sound is a **mechanical wave** — it needs particles to travel, so it cannot cross a vacuum, and it moves fastest where particles are packed tightest: solids beat liquids beat gases (about 343 metres per second in air). Humans hear 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second; below that is infrasound, above it is ultrasound. SONAR sends ultrasound into the sea and times the echo to measure depth. **Heat** moves in three ways: conduction through touching solids, convection by moving fluids (sea and land breezes), and radiation which needs no medium at all — that is how the Sun's heat crosses empty space. Water takes in a lot of heat for a small temperature rise (high specific heat), so it keeps coastal climates mild; **latent heat** is the heat a substance swallows to change state (ice to water) without its temperature rising.

**Picture it**

| Mode | Needs a medium? | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Conduction | yes (solids) | heating a metal rod |
| Convection | yes (fluids) | sea breeze, boiling water |
| Radiation | no (works in vacuum) | heat from the Sun |

**Terms explained**
- **Converging** — rays brought together to a point.
- **Diverging** — rays spread apart.
- **Dispersion** — splitting of white light into its colours (red to violet).
- **Ultrasound** — sound above 20,000 vibrations per second, too high for humans to hear.
- **Latent heat** — heat taken in or given out during a change of state, at constant temperature.

**Don't confuse**
- **Concave vs convex** — a concave mirror converges but a convex *lens* converges; the names behave oppositely for mirrors and lenses.
- **Ultrasound vs infrasound** — ultrasound is *above* 20,000 Hz (SONAR); infrasound is *below* 20 Hz.
- **Latent vs specific heat** — latent heat changes state at fixed temperature; specific heat changes temperature.

**Remember it**
"Radiation is the only heat that travels through nothing — that is why we feel the Sun."

**TL;DR**
- Concave mirror and convex lens converge; convex mirror and concave lens diverge; rear-view = convex mirror.
- A prism disperses white light into red-to-violet; refraction is light bending between media.
- Sound needs a medium, is fastest in solids; audible range 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; ultrasound (>20,000 Hz) drives SONAR.
- Heat: conduction (solids), convection (fluids), radiation (works in vacuum).
- Water's high specific heat moderates coastal climate; latent heat changes state at constant temperature.
keyPoints: Concave mirror converges (headlights, shaving); convex mirror diverges (rear-view, wide view).
Convex lens is converging and corrects hypermetropia; concave lens is diverging and corrects myopia.
A prism disperses white light into red-to-violet; refraction is the bending of light between media.
Sound needs a medium (no sound in vacuum) and travels fastest in solids; audible range 20 Hz-20 kHz.
Ultrasound (>20 kHz) is used in SONAR to measure sea depth; echo is reflected sound.
Heat transfer: conduction (solids), convection (fluids), radiation (works in vacuum, e.g. the Sun).
items.source: NCERT Science Class 9-10 — Light: Reflection and Refraction; Sound; Heat

items.title: Physics III — Electricity, Magnetism & Modern Physics
items.body:
### Electricity and magnetism

**In one line**
Electric current is the flow of charge through a circuit, and a changing magnet can create that current — the link that powers generators and motors.

**The story**
In a circuit, voltage pushes current through resistance, and Ohm found these are proportional: V = IR. Join components one after another (**series**) and the same current flows through each; join them side by side (**parallel**) and each gets the full voltage, which is how house wiring works so one switch does not kill the rest. A **fuse** is a thin wire placed *in series* in the live line; if too much current flows it heats up and melts, breaking the circuit before a fire starts. Oersted noticed a current makes a magnetic field, and Faraday found the reverse — moving a magnet near a coil *induces* a current. This two-way link is the heart of technology: a **generator** turns motion into electricity, and a **motor** turns electricity into motion.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
Ohm's law, 'is a fuse in series or parallel', and 'what is electromagnetic induction the basis of' are standard statement MCQs; power formulae and the kilowatt-hour unit also recur.

**Picture it**

| Idea | Fact |
|---|---|
| Ohm's law | V = IR (voltage = current × resistance) |
| Series circuit | same current everywhere; resistances add |
| Parallel circuit | same voltage across each; used in homes |
| Electric power | P = VI = I²R = V² ÷ R; energy sold in kilowatt-hours ('units') |
| Fuse / MCB | in series in the live wire; works by the heating effect of current |

### Modern physics — inside the atom

**The story (continued)**
An atom is a tiny nucleus of **protons and neutrons** surrounded by electrons. Some heavy nuclei are unstable and shoot out radiation: **alpha** (a helium nucleus), **beta** (an electron) or **gamma** (high-energy light). Two processes release huge energy: **fission**, where a heavy nucleus is split into lighter pieces — this runs every nuclear power reactor and the atom bomb; and **fusion**, where light nuclei are squeezed together into a heavier one — this powers the Sun and the hydrogen bomb. Controlled fusion on Earth is still experimental (projects such as ITER), so reactors today use fission only.

**Picture it**

| Emission | What it is |
|---|---|
| Alpha | a helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons) |
| Beta | a fast electron |
| Gamma | high-energy electromagnetic radiation |

**Terms explained**
- **Current (I)** — the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes.
- **Resistance (R)** — opposition to current, measured in ohms.
- **Electromagnetic induction** — producing a current by moving a magnet near a coil (Faraday).
- **Fission** — splitting a heavy nucleus; **Fusion** — joining light nuclei.
- **Kilowatt-hour** — the commercial 'unit' of electrical energy on your bill.

**Don't confuse**
- **Fission vs fusion** — fission *splits* (reactors, atom bomb); fusion *joins* (the Sun, hydrogen bomb).
- **Fuse: series not parallel** — it must carry the full current to break it, so it sits in series.
- **Generator vs motor** — generator makes electricity from motion; motor makes motion from electricity.

**Remember it**
"Fu**S**ion = **S**un and **S**tars (joining); fi**SS**ion = **S**plitting."

**TL;DR**
- Ohm's law V = IR; power P = VI = I²R; energy billed in kilowatt-hours.
- Series = same current; homes are wired in parallel; a fuse sits in series on the live wire.
- Electromagnetic induction (Faraday) is the basis of the generator; a motor converts electricity to motion.
- Radioactive emissions: alpha (helium nucleus), beta (electron), gamma (EM radiation).
- Fission (splitting) powers reactors; fusion (joining) powers the Sun.
keyPoints: Ohm's law: V = IR; electric power P = VI = I²R; commercial energy unit = kilowatt-hour.
In series the current is the same; household appliances are wired in parallel.
A fuse/MCB is connected in series in the live wire and works on the heating effect of current.
Electromagnetic induction (Faraday) is the basis of the generator; a motor converts electrical to mechanical energy.
Radioactive emissions: alpha (He nucleus), beta (electron), gamma (EM radiation).
Fission (heavy nucleus splits) powers reactors; fusion (light nuclei combine) powers the Sun.
items.source: NCERT Science Class 10 — Electricity; Magnetic Effects of Electric Current; Structure of the Atom

figure.caption: Radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-ray → gamma (rising frequency/energy).

items.title: Chemistry I — Matter, Atoms, Acids-Bases & Common Compounds
items.body:
### Matter and the atom

**In one line**
All stuff around us is matter, which we sort into elements, compounds and mixtures, and the atom is the smallest building block that decides how each behaves.

**The story**
Matter exists as solid, liquid or gas; some solids skip the liquid stage and turn straight to vapour (**sublimation**, as with camphor and dry ice). We classify matter by what it is made of: an **element** is one kind of atom (iron, oxygen), a **compound** is two or more elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio (water, carbon dioxide), and a **mixture** is substances merely mixed with no fixed ratio (air, sea water). A change that makes no new substance is **physical** (ice melting); one that makes a new substance is **chemical** (iron rusting, wood burning). Zoom in and every element is made of atoms: a nucleus of **protons** (which set the atomic number) and **neutrons**, circled by electrons. Atoms of the same element with different neutron counts are **isotopes** — same atomic number, different mass number.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
'Is air a compound or mixture?', 'is rusting physical or chemical?', atomic-number/mass-number definitions and the chemical names of household compounds are high-frequency APPSC items.

**Picture it**

| Type | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Element | one kind of atom | iron, oxygen, gold |
| Compound | elements chemically joined | water, carbon dioxide, common salt |
| Mixture | just mixed, no fixed ratio | air, sea water, soil |

### Acids, bases and common compounds

**The story (continued)**
Acids taste sour and release hydrogen ions; bases feel soapy and release hydroxide ions. The **pH scale** from 0 to 14 measures this: below 7 is acidic, exactly 7 is neutral (pure water), above 7 is basic. When an acid meets a base they cancel out — **neutralisation** — giving a salt and water. Many everyday substances are simple salts and compounds with well-known chemical names, and APPSC loves matching the common name to the formula.

**Picture it**

| Common name | Chemical name / formula |
|---|---|
| Common salt | sodium chloride, NaCl |
| Baking soda | sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO₃ |
| Washing soda | hydrated sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O |
| Bleaching powder | calcium oxychloride, CaOCl₂ |
| Quicklime | calcium oxide, CaO |
| Slaked lime | calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂ |
| Plaster of Paris | calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO₄·½H₂O |

**Terms explained**
- **Atomic number** — the number of protons in an atom; it defines the element.
- **Mass number** — protons plus neutrons.
- **Isotopes** — atoms of one element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers (carbon-12 and carbon-14).
- **Valency** — an atom's combining capacity (carbon's valency is 4, giving methane, CH₄).
- **pH** — a 0-to-14 number showing how acidic (<7) or basic (>7) a solution is.

**Don't confuse**
- **Air vs water** — air is a *mixture*; water is a *compound*.
- **Physical vs chemical change** — melting is physical (no new substance); rusting and burning are chemical.
- **Isotopes keep atomic number** — they differ in mass number (neutrons), not atomic number.
- **Baking soda vs washing soda** — baking soda is NaHCO₃; washing soda is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.

**Remember it**
"**Baking** soda = **bi**carbonate (NaHCO₃)"; and "pH **l**ow = acid, pH **h**igh = base".

**TL;DR**
- Air is a mixture; water and carbon dioxide are compounds; rusting and burning are chemical changes.
- Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons; isotopes share atomic number.
- Valency = combining capacity; carbon's is 4.
- pH below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic; acid + base → salt + water.
- Baking soda NaHCO₃, washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, bleaching powder CaOCl₂, quicklime CaO.
keyPoints: Air is a mixture; water and CO₂ are compounds; rusting and burning are chemical changes.
Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons; isotopes share atomic number, differ in mass.
Valency = combining capacity; carbon has valency 4.
pH < 7 acidic, 7 neutral, > 7 basic; acid + base → salt + water (neutralisation).
Baking soda = NaHCO₃, washing soda = Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, bleaching powder = CaOCl₂, quicklime = CaO.
Plaster of Paris = CaSO₄·½H₂O; slaked lime = Ca(OH)₂; common salt = NaCl.
items.mnemonic: 'Baking = Bicarbonate' → baking soda is sodium biCARBonate (NaHCO₃).
items.source: NCERT Science Class 9-10 — Matter; Atoms and Molecules; Acids, Bases and Salts

items.title: Chemistry II — Metals, Non-metals, Carbon Compounds & Fertilisers
items.body:
### Metals, non-metals and alloys

**In one line**
Metals are shiny, bendable conductors; non-metals are mostly dull insulators; mixing metals gives alloys with better properties.

**The story**
Metals shine, can be hammered into sheets (malleable) and drawn into wires (ductile), and conduct heat and electricity; **mercury** is the odd one out — the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Non-metals are generally brittle and poor conductors, with **graphite** the famous exception that conducts. The **noble (inert) gases** — helium, neon, argon and others — barely react, which is why an electric filament bulb is filled with **argon or nitrogen**: an unreactive atmosphere stops the white-hot tungsten filament from reacting with oxygen and burning out. Metals can be ranked by how eagerly they react (the **reactivity series**); gold and silver sit at the unreactive end, so they are called noble metals. Because a pure metal is not always ideal, we blend metals into **alloys** — brass, bronze and steel each gain strength or resistance from the mix.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
'Only liquid metal', alloy compositions, 'which gas fills a bulb and why', and the reactivity order are repeat APPSC single-fact and statement questions.

**Picture it**

| Alloy | Made from |
|---|---|
| Brass | copper + zinc |
| Bronze | copper + tin |
| Steel | iron + carbon |
| Stainless steel | iron + chromium + nickel |

Reactivity series (most to least reactive): K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au.

### Carbon compounds and fertilisers

**The story (continued)**
Carbon is special because it bonds with itself in long chains, so it forms millions of compounds. The same element can appear in different physical forms, called **allotropes**: diamond (hardest natural substance), graphite (soft and conducting), fullerene and graphene. **Hydrocarbons** are compounds of only carbon and hydrogen — methane (CH₄) is the simplest. **Polymers** are very long repeating chains: some are natural (cellulose, natural rubber, proteins), others synthetic (polythene, PVC, nylon, bakelite). Crops need three main nutrients, remembered as **NPK** — nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium; urea is the main nitrogen fertiliser.

**Terms explained**
- **Malleable** — can be hammered into thin sheets.
- **Ductile** — can be drawn into wires.
- **Alloy** — a mixture of a metal with other metals or carbon to improve its properties.
- **Allotropes** — different physical forms of the same element (diamond and graphite are both carbon).
- **Polymer** — a large molecule made of many repeating small units.

**Don't confuse**
- **Natural vs synthetic polymer** — cellulose and natural rubber are natural; polythene, PVC and nylon are synthetic.
- **Brass vs bronze** — brass is copper + zinc; bronze is copper + tin.
- **Diamond vs graphite** — same element (carbon), opposite properties: diamond is hard and non-conducting, graphite is soft and conducting.

**Remember it**
"**Bra**ss has **z**inc (Bra-Z); **bro**nze has **t**in"; crops want "**NPK** — Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium".

**TL;DR**
- Mercury is the only liquid metal; non-metals are poor conductors except graphite.
- Filament bulbs are filled with argon (or nitrogen) to stop the filament oxidising.
- Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au; gold and silver are noble.
- Brass = copper + zinc; bronze = copper + tin; steel = iron + carbon.
- Carbon allotropes diamond/graphite/fullerene/graphene; methane is the simplest hydrocarbon; fertilisers supply N-P-K (urea = nitrogen).
keyPoints: Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature; non-metals are poor conductors (except graphite).
Electric filament bulbs are filled with argon (or nitrogen), an inert gas, to prevent the filament from oxidising.
Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au; gold and silver are noble metals.
Brass = copper + zinc; bronze = copper + tin; steel = iron + carbon.
Carbon allotropes: diamond, graphite, fullerene, graphene; methane is the simplest hydrocarbon.
Polythene, PVC and nylon are synthetic polymers; cellulose and natural rubber are natural polymers.
Fertilisers supply N-P-K; urea is a nitrogenous fertiliser.
items.source: NCERT Science Class 10 — Metals and Non-metals; Carbon and its Compounds

items.title: Biology — Cell, Human Body, Nutrition & Plant Physiology
items.body:
### The cell and the human body

**In one line**
The cell is the basic unit of all life, and the human body is a team of organ systems each with its own working unit.

**The story**
Robert Hooke first saw box-like 'cells' in cork; later Robert Brown spotted the **nucleus**, the cell's control centre. Inside the cell, the **mitochondria** release energy and so are called the powerhouse, while ribosomes build proteins. Plant and animal cells differ in a few key parts — a plant cell has a rigid cell wall and green chloroplasts, which animal cells lack. In the body, each system has a basic unit and a headline fact worth memorising: the **neuron** runs the nervous system, the **nephron** filters the blood in the kidney, the lungs' **alveoli** exchange gases, and the **liver** is the largest gland. Blood comes in groups, with **O-negative** the universal donor and **AB** the universal recipient.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
'Powerhouse of the cell', 'largest gland', universal donor/recipient, and functional units (neuron, nephron) are among the most repeated science facts in APPSC and other PSC papers.

**Picture it**

| Feature | Plant cell | Animal cell |
|---|---|---|
| Cell wall | present | absent |
| Chloroplast | present | absent |
| Large vacuole | present | small or absent |

### Nutrition, hormones and plants

**The story (continued)**
Food supplies vitamins, and a shortage of each causes a specific **deficiency disease** — these matches are classic exam fodder. Chemical messengers called **hormones** keep the body balanced: insulin from the pancreas controls blood sugar, thyroxine from the thyroid controls metabolism (it needs iodine, and a shortage causes goitre), adrenaline is the fight-or-flight hormone, and the pituitary at the base of the brain is the 'master gland'. Green plants make their own food by **photosynthesis** — using sunlight, the green pigment chlorophyll turns carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen — and lose excess water as vapour through tiny leaf pores (**transpiration**). All living things are sorted by Whittaker's **five-kingdom** scheme.

**Picture it**

| Deficiency | Disease |
|---|---|
| Vitamin A | night blindness |
| Vitamin C | scurvy |
| Vitamin D | rickets |
| Vitamin B1 | beriberi |
| Iron | anaemia |
| Iodine | goitre |

**Terms explained**
- **Nucleus** — the control centre of the cell that holds its genetic material.
- **Mitochondria** — the cell's powerhouse, where energy is released.
- **Nephron** — the filtering unit of the kidney.
- **Hormone** — a chemical messenger released by a gland into the blood.
- **Photosynthesis** — how green plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight and chlorophyll.

**Don't confuse**
- **Cell wall vs cell membrane** — the rigid cell wall is only in plant cells; both plant and animal cells have a membrane.
- **Largest gland vs pancreas** — the liver is the largest gland; the pancreas is the second largest.
- **Neuron vs nephron** — neuron is the nerve unit; nephron is the kidney unit.
- **Universal donor vs recipient** — O-negative donates to all; AB receives from all.

**Remember it**
"**Mito**chondria = **might** (power) house"; five kingdoms spell **MPFPA** — Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.

**TL;DR**
- Robert Hooke saw cells; Robert Brown found the nucleus; mitochondria = powerhouse.
- Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts; animal cells lack both.
- Liver is the largest gland; alveoli exchange gases; O-negative = universal donor, AB = universal recipient.
- Deficiencies: Vitamin A → night blindness, C → scurvy, D → rickets, B1 → beriberi, iron → anaemia, iodine → goitre.
- Photosynthesis needs chlorophyll and sunlight; Whittaker's five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
keyPoints: Robert Hooke discovered cells (cork); Robert Brown discovered the nucleus; mitochondria = powerhouse.
Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts; animal cells lack both.
Liver is the largest gland; alveoli exchange gases; O-negative = universal donor, AB = universal recipient.
Neuron = nervous system unit; nephron = kidney unit; medulla controls heartbeat and breathing.
Deficiencies: Vitamin A→night blindness, C→scurvy, D→rickets, B1→beriberi, iron→anaemia, iodine→goitre.
Photosynthesis needs chlorophyll and light; Whittaker's five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.

items.title: For Mains — Science in daily life & scientific temper
items.body:
**In one line**
For Mains (Paper-5, clause M5-1 'S&T in daily life'), basic science is not recalled as facts but used to argue how scientific literacy improves health, safety, agriculture and governance.

**The analytical frame**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Significance | science literacy → safer homes, better health choices, higher farm yields, informed citizens |
| Everyday physics | electrical safety (fuse in series, earthing), optics (spectacles, mirrors), pressure cooker, solar cooker |
| Everyday chemistry | pH and acids/bases in cleaning and antacids, lime for water/soil, food-adulteration awareness |
| Everyday biology | balanced diet, vitamin-deficiency diseases, immunisation, hygiene lower the disease burden |
| Governance link | uptake of immunisation, salt iodisation, ORS, food fortification; countering misinformation and superstition |
| Criticism / limits | low science spend (~0.65% of GDP), rural awareness gaps, pseudoscience, poor last-mile communication |
| Way forward | school science reform, public-communication campaigns, Article 51A(h) scientific temper as a civic goal |

**Data, provisions and examples to quote**
- **Article 51A(h)** — developing scientific temper is a Fundamental Duty.
- India's R&D spend ≈ **0.65% of GDP** (target ~2%), below major economies — a standing criticism.
- Public-health wins rooted in basic science: **iodised salt** (goitre), **ORS** (diarrhoea), fortified mid-day meals, universal immunisation.
- **AP angle**: tackling **fluorosis** (high-fluoride groundwater in parts of Rayalaseema/Prakasam) and anaemia needs citizens to grasp water chemistry and nutrition; chlorination/defluoridation of drinking water.

**Use in answers**
- Open with Article 51A(h) to frame scientific temper as a constitutional value, not a slogan.
- Quote the 0.65%-of-GDP R&D figure to make a crisp 'way forward' (raise investment, strengthen communication).
- Diagram idea: a simple cycle — scientific literacy → better everyday choices → healthier, safer citizens → more effective governance.
- A usable line: "A citizen who understands pH, a fuse and a balanced diet is cheaper to govern and harder to mislead."
